title: What do the marked numbers in the table share?
description: A table of numbers from thirty one to seventy has some numbers shaded and some circled. The gaps show that the shaded numbers count in threes, the circled numbers count in fours, and the numbers with both marks are named. Keeko's doubt, that those numbers are factors, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: the step between marked numbers tells which multiples they are, and a number with both marks is a common multiple. Watch for students who call the doubly marked numbers factors because they are linked to three and four.

source: Look at the table below (numbers 31 to 70; shaded and circled numbers)
video_script.why: The child reads the step between the shaded numbers and between the circled numbers, and names the numbers that have both marks.
video_script.substitution: The step between neighbouring marked numbers is the number whose multiples they are.
video_script.anchor: the number table of the book, from thirty one to seventy, with some numbers shaded and some circled
video_script.wrong_answer: called factors of three and four
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the numbers with both marks are called factors of three and four. They are far bigger than three and four and come from counting on, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Thirty six, forty eight and sixty have both marks, and are common multiples of three and four

final_answer.spoken: thirty six, forty eight and sixty, the common multiples of three and four

never_show: the name common multiples before the answer
factors of 3 and 4 as the answer
maths_rules: shaded: 33, 36, 39, 42, 45, 48, 51, 54, 57, 60, 63, 66, 69; each is 3 more than the one before, so they are multiples of 3
circled: 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60, 64, 68; each is 4 more than the one before, so they are multiples of 4
the next one, 72, lies outside the table
slip: factors of 3 are 1 and 3, so 36, 48 and 60 are not factors of 3 or of 4
video_script.design: One idea: the step between marked numbers gives the multiples, and both marks make a common multiple. Assumes skip counting. Wrong idea: the doubly marked numbers are called factors. The table stays on the board to the end.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: shaded numbers 33, 36, 39, 42, 45, 48, ...; 36 - 33 = 3, 39 - 36 = 3, 42 - 39 = 3; so they are multiples of 3

marks.gap: each gap between neighbouring shaded numbers is marked as 3
marks.rule: the word multiples of 3 is written beside the shaded numbers

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step one, read the shaded numbers: thirty three, thirty six, thirty nine, forty two and on.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Thirty six take away thirty three is three. Thirty nine take away thirty six is three.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Each shaded number is three more than the one before. They are multiples of three.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: circled numbers 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, ...; 36 - 32 = 4, 40 - 36 = 4, 44 - 40 = 4; so they are multiples of 4

marks.list: the circled numbers are read out in order
marks.gap: each gap between neighbouring circled numbers is marked as 4
marks.rule: the word multiples of 4 is written beside the circled numbers

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step two, read the circled numbers: thirty two, thirty six, forty, forty four and on.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Thirty six take away thirty two is four. Forty take away thirty six is four.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Each circled number is four more than the one before. They are multiples of four.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: numbers with both marks: 36, 48, 60 (a shaded number that is also circled)

<bookmark mark='three'/>Thirty six, forty eight and sixty have both.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 36, 48 and 60 have both marks; they are the common multiples of 3 and 4

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Thirty six, forty eight and sixty have both marks, and are common multiples of three and four.
<bookmark mark='name'/>A number that is a multiple of two numbers at once is called a common multiple.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

marks.doubt: the bubble appears with the word factors

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the numbers with both marks are called factors of three and four.
<bookmark mark='far'/>But those numbers are much bigger than three and four, and they come from counting on.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Counting on gives multiples, so they are common multiples.
